This summer has been crazy for me and my garden got away from me. Bad drought and I didn't have time to care for it. Most of my tomatoes ended up in compost. But I'm not too sad. I sowed some cover crops where I plan on putting some flint corn next year (using seeds saved from this year's bloody butcher corn). I also planted some lettuce and fava beans.

This has been my first year saving seeds as well and I have butternut squash, 2 tomato varieties, the aforementioned corn, and okra. God damn I love gardening. I have also been stealing leaves and straw that the neighbor's throw out.
Any fellow gardeners here? What are you doing to prepare for winter?

I live in Phoenix so nothing. But for real it can get down into the mid 20's overnight here in January-February and I have a ton of herbs I either need to cover up or transfer to pots and put in the sun-room. I wish I could be more help but I'm a terrible gardener and still in the learning process myself, this is the first year I got anything to survive the 115* summer.
I lived in Tucson and that's where I first tried gardening. So much water needed during the summer, I had to quit.

This year we had a pretty meager garden because we were out of town for the planting season. Still, I've brought in all of the houseplants, checked on some of the potted plants we have outside, harvested the massive amount of basil we planted in lieu of anything else, and brought the rosemary in to try and keep it alive through the winter. I've also harvested a good amount of lemon balm (dried for tea), tidied up that plant a bit, taken care of the roses (all planted from cuttings this summer), and potted all of the cuttings I had lying around in the kitchen (french ivy, english ivy, spider plant, willow, some other sort of plant).

I still need to take care of the grape vines, till the garden, and there are two stumps I want to knock out. Then I need to move all of the remaining potted plants outside into the garden for overwintering.
How often do you till? Everything I read about it suggests it is terrible for the soil.

I don't do a deep till - 3 inches unless I'm trying to change soil composition (adding sand and/or peat) - then I'll do a full till. I till once early in the Spring, once right before planting, and once in the Fall.

We have really rich soil up here in New York, so YMMV.

What I've read has been more in relation to soil structure - that over-tilling or even regular tilling will eventually lead to compaction and hard-pan. If you're interested, you could google it. Just thought I would give it a mention.

I had taken a couple years off from the garden but decided to do it again this spring. My problem wasn't drought, it was too much water, and too much success. I cleaned out my chicken coop for the first time in about 3-4 years and added that to the first couple beds in the garden area. (For those curious as to why I hadn't cleaned out my coop, it was for two reasons. I just spread about a bale of wheat straw on the top of what is already on the floor when it starts smelling bad. That way my coop floor ends up being a big compost bin. The second reason is because I was to lazy to move it to an actual compost bin.)

I bought some tomato plants from local feed stores and BLAM, they went crazy with the chicken poop infused dirt. They easily reached 8 foot tall, both the cherry tomato and beefsteak varieties. They were so big I had no way to support them because I had never had any grow quite that vigorously. We were also having a very raining spring and I couldn't keep the grass under control because by the time it ever got dry enough on a weekend to work in the garden the grass had grown knee high again.

The nail in the coffin was we had a bad storm. The wind was so bad I was sure we were having a tornado pass through. Well no twister but the wind was strong enough to blow over my tomato plants, They were so massive and intertwined there was no way for me to stand them back up. This was after having to complete denude the garden of knee-high grass for the third time, so I just gave up. We got a couple more tomatoes but most of the time they were half rotten before they ripened because it had been so wet.

Currently the last of the tomato plants are dying, the grass is still growing thicker and I have foregone any fall crops. Maybe once a hard frost kills everything I will attack the ground with a tiller, or maybe I will just ignore it another couple years.
I had an overproduction of tomatoes as well this year. Next year I will only do 3 or 4 plants, not 15.
